sections.title: 6. How to Approach Any Digit DP Problem

blocks.text: Before patterns and code, let's understand what digit DP is and what kind of problem it solves.
Count how many numbers between 1 and N satisfy some condition.

items: How many numbers from 1 to 1000 have a digit sum equal to 10?
How many numbers from 1 to 10000 have no two consecutive digits that are the same?
How many numbers from 1 to N are divisible by the sum of their digits?

blocks.text: Brute force loop from 1 to N, check each number.
/engineering/dsa-media/1785406197843-461061338.png
Digit DP instead of checking every number, you build numbers digit by digit and count valid ones smartly.
Every number from 1 to N can be built one digit at a time, from left to right.
/engineering/dsa-media/1785406197843-195503050.png
Numbers you can build:

items:
First digit: 1, 2, 3
(cannot exceed 3 the first digit of N)

Second digit: 0, 1, 2, ...
(depends on what the first digit was)

blocks.text: At each position, the choice of digits is constrained by the corresponding digit of N only if the prefix built so far is equal to N’s prefix; otherwise, any digit (0–9) can be used.
The Tight Constraint
This is the most important concept in digit DP.
N = 357
Building digit by digit:
Position 0: choosing the first digit:

items:
If you choose 1 or 2 → you become FREE for the remaining digits
(any digit from 0–9 can be chosen going forward)

If you choose 3 → you remain TIGHT
(the next digit cannot exceed 5, the second digit of N)

blocks.text: Cleaner conceptual version:

items: FREE state: Once your constructed number is already smaller than N, you can use any digit (0–9) for all remaining positions.
TIGHT state: If your prefix matches N so far, the next digit is restricted by the corresponding digit of N.

blocks.text: The tight flag tells you  am I still bounded by N, or am I free?
/engineering/dsa-media/1785406197844-890892817.png
Once you go below N's digit at any position tight becomes false forever for that path.
/engineering/dsa-media/1785406197844-974829356.png
Digit-by-digit paths:

items:
Path: 2 → ? → ?
→ tight = false
→ All remaining digits can be 0–9

blocks.text: Clean intuition:

items: As long as your prefix exactly matches N → you stay tight (restricted).
The moment your prefix becomes smaller than N → you become free (no restrictions afterward).

blocks.text: Every digit DP problem has the same core state:
/engineering/dsa-media/1785406280356-880293497.png

Digit DP state:
dp[position][tight][state]

Here, position represents the current digit index (from 0 to len−1), tight indicates whether the current number is still bounded by N (true means restricted, false means free), and state represents any problem-specific information such as digit sum, last digit, count, remainder, etc.
In essence, you track where you are, whether you are restricted, and whatever additional information the problem requires.
The problem specific part changes based on what condition you're counting.
/engineering/dsa-media/1785406280357-969173227.png

Count numbers with digit sum = 10:
dp[position][tight][currentSum]

Count numbers with no consecutive equal digits:
dp[position][tight][lastDigit]

Count numbers divisible by K:
dp[position][tight][remainderSoFar]
<hr style="border-width: 1px medium medium; border-style: solid none none; border-color: rgb(224, 224, 224) currentcolor currentcolor; border-image: none; margin: 24px 0px;">
You convert N to its digit array first. Then you place digits one position at a time.

N = 357
digits = [3, 5, 7]

Position 0 → hundreds digit
Position 1 → tens digit
Position 2 → units digit
At each position:
limit = (tight) ? digits[position] : 9
Try each digit d from 0 to limit:

items: If d < digits[position] → next position becomes tight = false
If d == digits[position] → next position remains tight = true

blocks.text:
Key idea:

  • Once you pick a smaller digit → you become free
  • If you match exactly → you stay tight
The General Template
The structure never changes only thestateand theisValidlogic differ from problem to problem.
The Leading Zero Problem
One extra complication numbers like 007 are not valid three-digit numbers, so leading zeros need special handling.

codes.javascript:
Building the number 7 inside a 3-digit range:

Position 0: place 0  → not started yet  
Position 1: place 0  → still not started  
Position 2: place 7  → actual number starts here

blocks.text: To handle this, we track astartedflag whether a non-zero digit has been placed yet.
/engineering/dsa-media/1785406280357-676048840.png
Without memoization, you explore every possible digit sequence. For a number with d digits, that’s up to 10ᵈ paths.
With memoization, two calls with the same(position, tight, state)always produce the same result, so you cache and reuse them.

codes.javascript:
Total unique states:
   positions → at most 18 (for N up to 10^18)
   tight     → 2 values (true or false)
   state     → depends on problem (e.g., digit sum ≤ 162, last digit ≤ 9)

Total states → 18 × 2 × (state range) → manageable

blocks.text: Counting in a Range [L, R]
Most problems ask for a range [L, R], not just [1, N].
Use this trick:
Solve the problem twice:
Then subtract the results.

content.title: 6. How to Approach Any Digit DP Problem

blocks.text:
Step 1: Identify what you are counting
Numbers that satisfy some digit-based condition

Step 2: Define your state
position + tight + any required condition

Step 3: Handle leading zeros
Add a started flag if zeros affect validity

Step 4: Write the recurrence
Try each digit from 0 to limit, update the state, and pass the new tight value forward

Step 5: Handle range queries
Use count(R) − count(L − 1) for problems on range [L, R]

Core takeaway:

The structure remains the same only the state and transition logic change
